newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Asian Metals - China aluminium demand seen picking up.
newsitem.headline: Asian Metals - China aluminium demand seen picking up.

text.p: China's demand for aluminium was picking up slowly and buyers were looking for delivery of material soon after the Chinese New Year holiday on February 7-9, metals traders in Hong Kong said on Monday.
China was buying small packages of aluminium in lots of several thousand tonnes for delivery after Chinese New Year, they said.
Chinese premium bids were around US$65-$75 per tonne over the London Metal Exchange (LME) cash price, traders said.
Another metal trader noted that China's domestic aluminium prices were inching up and had firmed to 14,400 yuan ($1,735) per tonne from 13,700 yuan ($1,650) in the last quarter of 1996.
"This shows that demand is strengthening," he said, adding that an earlier contract was being delivered.
"The last lot (before the Chinese New Year), about 5,000 metric tonnes of aluminium ingots from the CIS, will arrive within 10 days at Guangzhou," he said.
The premium for the shipment was about $60 over the LME cash price, he said.
In other base metal markets, zinc premiums remained at around $110-$120 and were not expected to change for the whole first quarter of 1997, a zinc metal dealer said.
"This is because most long-term contracts have been fixed already and the spot prices should follow the contract prices," the metals trader said.

China's Jinlong copper smelter project in Anhui province will start production on February 28, a spokesman for Sumitomo Metal Mining Co, a 20-percent owner of the project, told Reuters in Tokyo on Monday.
A Hong Kong trader who supplies copper to the project said his firm had shipped 10,000 tonnes of copper concentrate from Chile's Escondida mine late in December.
His company had a contract with the smelter in China, he said but did not give details.

"The Japanese management told us they are very comfortable with equipment and they would like to go in earlier, but the Chinese management decided to go according to schedule because if anything goes wrong the equipment suppliers would suffer," he said.
